content: The interquartile range (IQR) for the number of HBsAg-positive participants per study was 307 to 1871, with a range spanning from 3 to 135,395 participants. The most frequently described models in the studies were those conducted within the last five years. Approximately 40% of studies reported the initiation of antiviral therapy (AVT) among eligible patients, while 47% documented viral load suppression among patients receiving AVT. However, 22% of studies did not adequately report data on patients lost to follow-up. Among seven randomized controlled trials, the overall risk of bias was low in four studies, associated with some concerns in three studies, and high in one study. The high risk of bias was primarily linked to missing outcome data. The rates of treatment eligibility assessment following hepatitis B virus (HBV) diagnosis were highly variable, even after stratification by models of care. Community-based testing showed a treatment eligibility assessment rate of 71%. However, diagnostic costs, particularly for HBV DNA quantification, were a significant barrier in some settings. The proportion of eligible individuals initiating AVT was also heterogeneous, with rates approaching 100% in large tertiary centers in the United States and the Netherlands. Retention in care was not associated with factors such as country income classification, cirrhosis prevalence, sample size, or study design. Five studies from specialist centers reported retention rates among patients who had not started AVT, with a retention rate of 66% in this group. Retention was significantly lower among those not receiving AVT compared to those who had initiated treatment within the same clinic. The overall care cascade for HBV demonstrated significant gaps, with losses of 15–28% at each step of the cascade in hospital-based specialist care models. These losses were particularly pronounced in retention among individuals not receiving AVT. In primary care or co-managed care models, even greater losses were observed at the stages of eligibility assessment, AVT initiation, and retention in care. Community-based studies with interventional designs showed improved linkage rates following diagnosis and consistently high rates of AVT initiation. However, data on retention in care and viral load suppression were lacking in these studies. The findings highlight the need for improved strategies to address gaps in the HBV care cascade, particularly in retention and treatment initiation, to achieve better outcomes for individuals living with hepatitis B.
